beats.character_japanese: いいですよ。体を洗ってから入ってくださいね。
beats.japanese_answer: わかりました。

beats.context_line: You're not sure which changing room is which.
beats.english_cue: Ask where the men's changing room is.
beats.japanese_answer: だんせいのほうはどこですか？
beats.romaji: Dansei no hou wa doko desu ka?

beats.context_line: Noriko points to the left door. You bow and head in.
beats.character_japanese: こちらですよ。ゆっくりどうぞ。
beats.japanese_answer: ありがとうございます。

key_phrases.note: はじめて (hajimete) means 'for the first time'. Adding んですが at the end (explained situation + trailing softener) is the polite way to flag that you're a newcomer and might need guidance. It's like saying 'the thing is, this is my first time...' — it invites help without asking directly.

key_phrases.phrase: シャンプーは持ち込めますか
key_phrases.meaning: Can I bring my own shampoo?
key_phrases.note: 持ち込む (mochikomu) means to bring something in from outside. 持ち込めますか uses the potential form — 'is it possible to bring in?' Most sento provide soap but not shampoo, and many sell it at the counter. Bringing your own is usually fine.

key_phrases.phrase: 体を洗ってから入ってください
key_phrases.reading: karada wo aratte kara haitte kudasai
key_phrases.meaning: Please wash your body before getting in
key_phrases.note: This is the core rule of any Japanese bath — you wash yourself at a shower station first, then soak in the communal tub. ～てから means 'after doing ~'. Noriko may say this to any first-timer, foreign or Japanese.

title: Temple Morning
scene_intro: You're up early and the streets are still quiet. A Buddhist temple sits behind a low stone wall, half-hidden by ginkgo trees. A young monk named Ryusei is sweeping the courtyard path with a wide bamboo broom. He looks up with a calm, open expression as you pass the gate and hesitate.
other_character: Ryusei, a young monk in his twenties
goal: light incense and draw an omikuji fortune slip
grammar_focus: ～てもいいですか, これは何ですか, どういう意味ですか, ～といいます
setting: a Buddhist temple, early morning

beats.context_line: Ryusei looks up from sweeping as you approach.
beats.character_japanese: おはようございます。
beats.japanese_answer: おはようございます。

beats.context_line: You see the incense urn near the main hall. Smoke drifts upward.
beats.english_cue: Ask if you may offer some incense.
beats.japanese_answer: お線香をあげてもいいですか？
beats.romaji: Osenko wo agete mo ii desu ka?

beats.context_line: Ryusei says of course. He shows you the incense sticks and explains how to light them and fan out the flame.
beats.character_japanese: もちろんです。火をつけて、手でけして、けむりをあびてください。
beats.english_cue: Thank him and ask what you should pray for — or can you pray for anything?
beats.japanese_answer: ありがとうございます。何でも祈っていいですか？
beats.romaji: Arigatou gozaimasu. Nandemo inotte ii desu ka?

beats.context_line: Ryusei says yes, anything you like. You offer the incense and bow. Afterward, you notice the omikuji box.
beats.english_cue: Ask if you may draw a fortune slip.
beats.japanese_answer: おみくじをひいてもいいですか？
beats.romaji: Omikuji wo hiite mo ii desu ka?

beats.context_line: Ryusei nods and guides you. You draw a slip. It says 大吉 at the top.
beats.character_japanese: 大吉ですね！いい運勢です。
beats.japanese_answer: 大吉はどういう意味ですか？
beats.romaji: Daikichi wa dou iu imi desu ka?

beats.context_line: Ryusei says it's the best fortune — great luck. He says you can take it with you or tie it to the rack.
beats.character_japanese: 一番いい運勢です。持って帰ってもいいし、あそこに結んでもいいですよ。
beats.english_cue: Say you'll take it home. Thank him.
beats.japanese_answer: 持って帰ります。ありがとうございました。

key_phrases.phrase: お線香をあげてもいいですか
key_phrases.reading: osenko wo agete mo ii desu ka
key_phrases.note: お線香 (osenko) is the word for incense sticks at a temple or shrine. あげる here means 'to offer (to the Buddha)'. ～てもいいですか is asking permission — 'is it okay if I do this?' Ryusei will say yes and tell you how.

key_phrases.phrase: おみくじをひいてもいいですか
key_phrases.reading: omikuji wo hiite mo ii desu ka
key_phrases.meaning: May I draw a fortune slip?
key_phrases.note: おみくじ are paper fortune slips drawn by shaking a container of numbered sticks. You draw a stick, get a number, find the matching slip. Results range from 大吉 (great luck) to 凶 (bad luck). ひく (to draw/pull) is the verb used for this.

意味 (imi) means meaning. どういう is 'what kind of / what sort of'. This question unlocks explanations everywhere — not just temples. When you see a word or sign you don't understand: これはどういう意味ですか? is polite and natural.

title: Local Bus
scene_intro: You need to get to the station but the trains don't run this way. There's a local bus. You get on at a stop you found on Google Maps — but the payment machine is unfamiliar and you're not sure where to get off. An older woman named Fumiko is sitting in the seat across the aisle, reading a newspaper.
other_character: Fumiko, a friendly older woman
goal: figure out how to pay and find out where to get off for the station
grammar_focus: ～に行きますか, どこで降りますか, 教えてもらえますか, あと何分ですか
setting: a local community bus, mid-morning

beats.context_line: You get on the bus. The machine by the driver looks unfamiliar.
beats.english_cue: Ask the driver how to pay.
beats.japanese_answer: すみません、どうやって払いますか？

beats.context_line: The driver explains you pay when you get off, or use Suica. You find a seat next to Fumiko.
beats.character_japanese: おりるときに払ってください。
beats.japanese_answer: わかりました。ありがとうございます。

beats.context_line: You turn to Fumiko. You need to get to the station.
beats.english_cue: Ask where you should get off for the station.
beats.japanese_answer: えきにはどこで降りればいいですか？
beats.romaji: Eki ni wa doko de orireba ii desu ka?

beats.context_line: Fumiko says get off at the third stop — 'Ekimae'.
beats.character_japanese: 三つ目のバス停、駅前で降りてください。
beats.english_cue: Ask about how many minutes it is.
beats.japanese_answer: あと何分くらいですか？

beats.context_line: She says about seven or eight minutes.
beats.character_japanese: 七、八分くらいですよ。
beats.english_cue: Ask if she can let you know when you get there.
beats.japanese_answer: 着いたら教えてもらえますか？

beats.context_line: Fumiko says of course. A few minutes later she taps your arm — this is your stop.
beats.character_japanese: はい、もちろん。…あ、ここですよ！
beats.japanese_answer: ありがとうございます！さようなら。

key_phrases.phrase: どこで降りればいいですか
key_phrases.reading: doko de orireba ii desu ka
key_phrases.note: 降りる (oriru) means to get off (a bus, train). ～れば～いいですか is a very useful pattern — 'what should I do to achieve X?' It's asking for advice on the best action. ～ればいいですか literally: 'if I do ~, will that be okay?'

key_phrases.meaning: Could you let me know? / Could you tell me?
key_phrases.note: 教える (oshieru) means to tell/teach. ～てもらえますか is a wonderfully polite way to ask someone to do something — more of a favour than a command. 着いたら教えてもらえますか? = 'could you let me know when we arrive?' Always works.

key_phrases.phrase: あと何分くらいですか
key_phrases.meaning: About how many minutes from here?
key_phrases.note: あと = remaining. 何分 (nan-pun) = how many minutes. くらい = approximately. Together: 'about how many minutes left?' The same formula works for stops (あと何駅) or any remaining quantity.

title: Taxi Ride
scene_intro: It's late. You've missed the last train and you need to get back to your neighbourhood. You find a taxi at the rank outside the station — a white cab with a green light glowing in the window. The driver, Tanaka, is a man in his sixties with a relaxed manner and white gloves. He presses a button and the door swings open automatically.
other_character: Tanaka, a calm and experienced taxi driver
goal: give your destination and have a short conversation on the way
grammar_focus: ～までおねがいします, ～のほうに, おまかせします, どのくらいかかりますか
setting: a taxi, late at night in Tokyo

beats.context_line: You get in. Tanaka turns around slightly.
beats.character_japanese: どちらまで？
beats.english_cue: Say you'd like to go to Sangenjaya.
beats.japanese_answer: 三軒茶屋までお願いします。

beats.context_line: Tanaka sets off. He asks which route you'd prefer — via the expressway or the normal road.
beats.character_japanese: 高速道路と下道、どちらがよろしいですか？
beats.english_cue: Say you'll leave it to him.
beats.japanese_answer: おまかせします。

beats.context_line: Tanaka nods and takes the expressway. He asks how long you've been in Japan.
beats.character_japanese: 日本は長いんですか？
beats.japanese_answer: 三ヶ月くらいです。

beats.context_line: Tanaka says that's still early days. He asks how you find Japan.
beats.character_japanese: 日本はどうですか？
beats.english_cue: Say you love it — everyone is very kind.
beats.japanese_answer: 大好きです。みんなとても親切ですね。
beats.romaji: Daisuki desu. Minna totemo shinsetsu desu ne.

beats.context_line: Tanaka smiles at that. You're pulling up to Sangenjaya.
beats.character_japanese: 着きましたよ。
beats.japanese_answer: おいくらですか？

beats.context_line: Tanaka says two thousand two hundred yen. You hand over the money.
beats.character_japanese: にせんにひゃくえんです。
beats.english_cue: Pay and say thank you and good night.
beats.japanese_answer: はい、どうぞ。ありがとうございました。おやすみなさい。

key_phrases.note: まで marks a destination or endpoint — 'as far as / up to'. ～までお願いします is THE phrase for getting a taxi anywhere. 渋谷までお願いします (to Shibuya please), ホテルまでお願いします (to the hotel please). Clean, polite, works every time.

key_phrases.meaning: I'll leave it to you / Your choice
key_phrases.note: まかせる means to leave something in someone else's hands. おまかせ is a respectful/humble version. In a taxi: 'take the route you prefer'. In a restaurant: the chef's choice. Saying おまかせします is often received as an expression of trust — it's a very Japanese move.

Taxi drivers are notorious for friendly small talk. どうですか is one of the most versatile questions in Japanese — 'how is it? / what do you think of it?' A warm, open-ended opener they'll appreciate you asking back.

title: Bookshop
scene_intro: You're in a multi-floor bookshop in Shibuya. The ground floor is magazines and stationery; somewhere up above is the manga section — you think. You need to find it, and ideally get a recommendation for something you can actually read with your current Japanese. A young member of staff named Eri is reorganising a display near the lift.
other_character: Eri, a bookseller in her mid-twenties
goal: find the manga section, get a beginner recommendation, and buy it
grammar_focus: ～はどこですか, 初心者, ふりがながついている, おすすめ
setting: a large bookshop in Shibuya

beats.context_line: You approach Eri near the lift.
beats.english_cue: Excuse her and ask where the manga section is.
beats.japanese_answer: すみません、マンガのコーナーはどこですか？
beats.romaji: Sumimasen, manga no koona wa doko desu ka?

beats.context_line: Eri says it's on the fourth floor. She offers to show you.
beats.character_japanese: 四階です。ご案内しますよ。
beats.english_cue: Say thank you, that would be great.
beats.japanese_answer: ありがとうございます。お願いします。

beats.context_line: You're in the manga section. It's enormous. Eri asks what you're looking for.
beats.character_japanese: どんなマンガをお探しですか？
beats.english_cue: Say you're a beginner in Japanese and want something with furigana.
beats.japanese_answer: 日本語は初心者なので、ふりがながついているものがいいです。
beats.romaji: Nihongo wa shoshinsha na node, furigana ga tsuite iru mono ga ii desu.

beats.context_line: Eri walks you to a shelf and pulls out a volume. She says this one is good for beginners.
beats.character_japanese: これはいかがですか？初心者の方に人気ですよ。
beats.english_cue: Ask if it will help with studying Japanese.
beats.japanese_answer: 日本語の勉強になりますか？
beats.romaji: Nihongo no benkyou ni narimasu ka?

beats.context_line: Eri says yes — the dialogue is simple and the furigana is thorough.
beats.character_japanese: はい、セリフがかんたんで、ふりがなもしっかりついていますよ。
beats.japanese_answer: じゃあ、これをください。

beats.context_line: Eri takes you to the register. She tells you the price — eight hundred yen.
beats.character_japanese: はっぴゃくえんです。
beats.japanese_answer: はい、どうぞ。ありがとうございました。

key_phrases.phrase: マンガのコーナーはどこですか
key_phrases.reading: manga no koona wa doko desu ka
key_phrases.note: コーナー (koona) from English 'corner' is used in Japanese shops to mean a dedicated section or zone. You'll see it on signs: 文房具コーナー (stationery), 料理コーナー (cookery). Using the English word in Japanese is completely natural here.

key_phrases.phrase: ふりがながついているものがいいです
key_phrases.reading: furigana ga tsuite iru mono ga ii desu
key_phrases.meaning: Something with furigana would be good
key_phrases.note: ふりがな are the small hiragana readings printed above or beside kanji. For learners they're gold — you can read the kanji even when you don't know the reading. Many manga aimed at children have them. Asking for furigana-equipped manga is a very sensible move.

key_phrases.phrase: 日本語の勉強になりますか
key_phrases.reading: Nihongo no benkyou ni narimasu ka
key_phrases.meaning: Will it help with studying Japanese?
key_phrases.note: 勉強になる literally means 'it becomes studying' — i.e., it's educational / a learning experience. This is a natural, often-used expression for saying something is informative or instructive. You can say it when you learn something from anyone: 勉強になりました (that was educational, thank you).

title: Neighbour Chat
scene_intro: You're heading out on a Tuesday morning, keys in hand, when your next-door neighbour opens his door at the same moment. It's Yamada-san — you've seen him a few times in the hallway but never really spoken. He's a man in his late fifties, neatly dressed, carrying an empty bottle bag for recycling. He smiles.
other_character: Yamada-san, your friendly next-door neighbour
goal: have a warm first proper conversation with your neighbour
grammar_focus: はじめまして, ～に住んでいます, 慣れてきました, なにかあれば
setting: the corridor outside your apartment, a Tuesday morning

beats.context_line: Yamada-san's door opens at the same moment as yours.
beats.character_japanese: あ、おはようございます！
beats.japanese_answer: おはようございます！

beats.context_line: Yamada-san smiles. It seems you haven't properly introduced yourselves yet.
beats.character_japanese: いつもお世話になっています。山田です。
beats.japanese_answer: こちらこそ。（名前）です。よろしくお願いします。
beats.romaji: Kochira koso. (namae) desu. Yoroshiku onegai shimasu.

beats.context_line: Yamada-san asks how long you've been in the building.
beats.character_japanese: こちらに越してきて、どのくらいになりますか？
beats.japanese_answer: 二ヶ月くらいになります。

beats.context_line: He asks if you've gotten used to the area.
beats.character_japanese: このへんには慣れましたか？
beats.english_cue: Say yes, you've gotten quite used to it.
beats.japanese_answer: はい、だいぶ慣れてきました。

beats.context_line: Yamada-san nods and mentions there's a good supermarket nearby.
beats.character_japanese: 近くにいいスーパーがありますよ。
beats.english_cue: Say you know it — you go there every week.
beats.japanese_answer: ええ、知っています。毎週行っています。
beats.romaji: Ee, shitte imasu. Maishuu itte imasu.

beats.context_line: Yamada-san wraps up warmly. He's heading to the recycling station.
beats.character_japanese: なにかあればいつでも。よろしくお願いします。
beats.english_cue: Thank him and say likewise — nice to meet you.
beats.japanese_answer: ありがとうございます。こちらこそ、よろしくお願いします。
beats.romaji: Arigatou gozaimasu. Kochira koso, yoroshiku onegai shimasu.

key_phrases.phrase: いつもお世話になっています
key_phrases.meaning: Thank you for everything / I'm always in your care
key_phrases.note: This is a ritual phrase in Japan — you say it to neighbours, colleagues, business contacts, even people you've barely met. It literally means 'I am always receiving your care', but it functions as a warm social lubricant. Yamada-san will say it too. Saying it back is the expected and appreciated move.

key_phrases.phrase: だいぶ慣れてきました
key_phrases.meaning: I'm getting used to it / I've settled in quite a bit
key_phrases.note: 慣れる (nareru) means to get used to / become accustomed to. ～てきました shows a process that's been happening over time and is approaching the present — 'I've gradually been getting used to it'. だいぶ means 'quite a bit / considerably'.

key_phrases.phrase: なにかあればいつでも
key_phrases.meaning: Any time if you need anything
key_phrases.note: なにかあれば = 'if there's anything (you need)'. いつでも = 'any time'. Together: 'any time you need anything (I'm here)'. This is the Japanese neighbourly offer — Yamada-san will likely say this to you. You can reply: ありがとうございます、よろしくお願いします.

title: Lost Umbrella
scene_intro: You left your umbrella on the train. A black folding one — nothing special, but it's raining right now and you need it. You find the lost property window at the station. A young station worker named Kenji slides open the frosted glass panel and looks at you expectantly.
other_character: Kenji, a polite young station worker
goal: report your lost umbrella and hopefully get it back
grammar_focus: 落とし物, 電車の中に忘れました, どんな～ですか, こちらですか
setting: the lost property window at a Tokyo train station

beats.context_line: Kenji slides open the window.
beats.character_japanese: はい、どうぞ。
beats.english_cue: Say you left something on the train.
beats.japanese_answer: 電車の中に忘れてしまいました。
beats.romaji: Densha no naka ni wasurete shimaimashita.

beats.context_line: Kenji takes out a form. He asks what you left.
beats.character_japanese: 何を忘れましたか？
beats.japanese_answer: 傘です。

beats.context_line: Kenji asks what kind of umbrella.
beats.character_japanese: どんな傘ですか？
beats.english_cue: Say it's a black folding umbrella.
beats.japanese_answer: 黒いおりたたみ傘です。

beats.context_line: Kenji asks which line you were on.
beats.character_japanese: どちらの路線でしたか？
beats.japanese_answer: 中央線です。

beats.context_line: Kenji disappears for a moment and comes back with a black folding umbrella.
beats.character_japanese: こちらですか？
beats.japanese_answer: はい、そうです！ありがとうございます。

beats.context_line: Kenji asks you to sign a form to confirm you've collected it.
beats.character_japanese: こちらにサインをお願いします。
beats.english_cue: Say of course, and thank him sincerely.
beats.japanese_answer: はい、わかりました。本当にありがとうございます。
beats.romaji: Hai, wakarimashita. Hontou ni arigatou gozaimasu.

key_phrases.phrase: 電車の中に忘れてしまいました
key_phrases.reading: densha no naka ni wasurete shimaimashita
key_phrases.meaning: I left it behind on the train
key_phrases.note: 忘れる (wasureru) means to forget or leave behind. ～てしまいました adds a sense of regret — something happened that you didn't intend. It's the natural thing to say for accidental mishaps. 電車の中に = on / inside the train. に marks the location where the leaving happened.

key_phrases.phrase: 黒いおりたたみ傘です
key_phrases.note: 折りたたみ (oritatami) means folding — from 折る (to fold) + たたむ (to fold flat). 傘 (kasa) is umbrella. When describing a lost item, you'll need colour + type + any distinguishing features. Kenji will ask you exactly this.

Short and essential. When someone shows you something to confirm it's yours, this is what they ask. Your answer: はい、そうです (yes, that's it) or ちがいます (that's not it). Simple confirming and denying questions like this are high-frequency in real interactions.

title: Hanami Picnic
scene_intro: It's late March and the sakura are out. Every bench and blue tarp in the park is taken. You're walking along the riverbank with a can of coffee when two students, Akira and Misa, sitting on a tarp nearby call out to you. They've got food, drinks, and more space than they need.
other_character: Akira and Misa, two friendly Japanese university students
goal: join their hanami picnic, share food, make a toast, and chat
grammar_focus: きれいですね, ～はじめてですか, よかったら, かんぱい
setting: a riverside park in Tokyo, late March, sakura in full bloom

beats.context_line: Akira waves at you from the tarp.
beats.character_japanese: ねえ！よかったら一緒にどうですか？
beats.english_cue: Accept enthusiastically — say you'd love to.
beats.japanese_answer: ありがとうございます！ぜひ。

beats.context_line: You sit down. Misa hands you a can of beer. You look up at the blossoms.
beats.english_cue: Say how beautiful the cherry blossoms are.
beats.japanese_answer: 桜、きれいですね！

beats.context_line: Akira asks if it's your first time at a hanami.
beats.character_japanese: 花見ははじめてですか？
beats.english_cue: Say yes, it's your very first one.
beats.japanese_answer: はい、はじめてのお花見です。

beats.context_line: Misa smiles and says welcome to Japan. She holds up her can.
beats.character_japanese: じゃあ、かんぱいしましょう！
beats.english_cue: Raise your drink and say cheers!
beats.japanese_answer: かんぱい！

beats.context_line: Akira offers you some onigiri from a box.
beats.character_japanese: おにぎり、どうぞ。
beats.english_cue: Accept gratefully and say it looks delicious.
beats.japanese_answer: ありがとうございます。おいしそうですね！

beats.context_line: Misa asks if you like Japan in spring.
beats.character_japanese: 春の日本、どうですか？
beats.english_cue: Say it's the best — especially the sakura.
beats.japanese_answer: 最高です。特に桜が好きです。
beats.romaji: Saikou desu. Toku ni sakura ga suki desu.

beats.context_line: They both laugh and say they're glad you like it. Akira raises his can again.
beats.character_japanese: また来年もどうぞ！かんぱい！
beats.english_cue: Raise your drink and say cheers again.
beats.japanese_answer: かんぱい！

key_phrases.phrase: よかったら一緒にどうですか
key_phrases.reading: yokattara issho ni dou desu ka
key_phrases.meaning: If you'd like, how about joining us?
key_phrases.note: よかったら is a beautiful soft invitation — 'if it's alright with you / if you'd like to'. It's tentative and non-pressuring, which is very Japanese. One of the most useful social phrases you can have. よかったら食べてください (please eat if you'd like), よかったら来てください (come if you'd like).

key_phrases.phrase: はじめてのお花見です
key_phrases.note: お花見 (ohanami) — flower viewing — is one of Japan's most beloved seasonal traditions. Sitting under the cherry blossoms with food and drinks, often in a group. Saying it's your first will be received with genuine warmth and probably some pride from your hosts.

かんぱい (kanpai) comes from 乾杯 — literally 'dry cup'. It's a toast, used the same way as 'cheers' in English. You clink drinks (or just raise them) and say it together. Drink whatever you're holding — no one cares if it's sparkling water or beer.
